profileSections.heading: Making room for children and families
profileSections.text: Israel “Izzy” David Andrews’s Arizona Dermatology biography describes an interest in expanding access to dermatologic care for children. Alongside his practice, it names community outreach and volunteering with underserved populations as part of his work. The account emphasizes following children as they grow into young adults, rather than treating each visit as an isolated encounter. Outside medicine, it describes travel, staying active, an interest in nutrition, and time with his two children. These are the practice’s published statements about his priorities and interests; they do not establish free-care eligibility, appointment availability or patient outcomes.

profileSections.heading: Before arranging care
profileSections.text: His named biography lists medical and pediatric dermatology and the Phoenix office at 2224 W. Northern Avenue, Suite D-300, phone 602-277-1449, with a Request Appointment route. Confirm age eligibility and the location when calling; a separate Scottsdale office is also listed. Current capacity, fees, plan-specific coverage, referral requirements and interpreter availability have not been established; confirm directly with the practice.

profileSections.heading: Trails, baking, and a large puzzle
profileSections.text: Linda Fancher’s Epiphany Dermatology biography offers a few concrete details of life beyond the office: hiking, baking, and tackling huge jigsaw puzzles. It also records that she has practiced dermatology in Honolulu since 1995. The interests are modest but specific, giving a glimpse of the person without turning her training into a résumé-style story. Her biography does not say that solving puzzles makes her a better diagnostician, or that these hobbies shape her care; no such connection is inferred here.

profileSections.heading: A morning swim, and years spent teaching
profileSections.text: Matthew Kanzler’s Epiphany Dermatology biography describes a morning routine in Waikiki: swimming with a group of fellow swimmers. It calls him a lifelong competitive swimmer, a personal interest that continues alongside his work in dermatology. The same biography recalls years at Santa Clara Valley Medical Center and a role directing Stanford’s dermatology residency program. That gives his published story two specific threads—time in the water with a community and time helping train physicians. The account is not evidence of better clinical results, and historical teaching appointments are not presented as verified current roles.
